a: I hear a speech I had never known:
p: The Hebrew has "I hear a speech I did not know"; the Greek and Syriac have "he heard a language he did not know".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew audivi
readings.en: a speech I did not know I hear
readings.plain: I hear a speech I had never known:

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 80:6); Gallican Psalter audivit; Syriac, as reported in BHS (not checked myself)
readings.en: a language he did not know, he heard
readings.plain: he heard a language he had never known:

why: The first person is the harder reading, and it introduces the oracle that follows: the singer hears a voice he does not recognize, God's. The Greek made the line part of the Joseph story (Joseph in Egypt heard a strange tongue), which the Targum and Rashi also tell in their own way.

t: "He would feed him" or "I would feed him"?
p: The Hebrew shifts from "he" to "I" in this verse. Many read "I would feed him"; the Greek has "he" both times.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: He would feed him

readings.w: Conjecture adopted by many modern translations
readings.plain: I would feed him

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 80:17); Gallican Psalter
readings.en: and he fed them ... he satisfied them
readings.plain: He fed them

why: Shifts of person are common in the psalms, and the Hebrew may be quoting Deuteronomy 32:13, "he fed him" (honey from the rock). The Plain keeps the Hebrew and the change of voice; the Greek smoothed it the other way. The tense is interpreted too: wayya'akhilehu is a past narrative form ("and he fed him"), which the Plain reads as part of the conditional promise of 81:13–16.

p: The Hebrew has "the assembly of El"; the Greek and Latin have "the assembly of gods".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: in the assembly of El

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 81:1); Gallican Psalter in synagoga deorum
readings.plain: in the assembly of gods

readings.w: Targum (checked myself)
readings.en: in the assembly of the righteous
readings.plain: in the assembly of the righteous

why: "El" here may be God's name or simply "divine" ("the divine assembly"); either way the council is God's. The Greek's "gods" interprets the same sense; the Targum's "the righteous" makes the gods human judges. See the notes on 82:1.

t: "No rest for you" or "Who is like you?"
p: The Greek read the first Hebrew word as "likeness", not "silence": "God, who will be likened to you?" The rest matches.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew
readings.plain: God, give yourself no rest!

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 82:2); Gallican Psalter Deus quis similis erit tibi
readings.orig: Ὁ θεός, τίς ὁμοιωθήσεταί σοι; μὴ σιγήσῃς μηδὲ καταπραΰνῃς, ὁ θεός
readings.en: God, who will be likened to you? Do not be silent, do not be calmed, O God
readings.plain: God, who will be compared with you? Do not be silent! Do not be still, O God!

why: Both have three clauses. The Greek tis homoiōthēsetai soi renders al-domi lakh, reading domi from damah, "be like", instead of "silence, rest"; mē sigēsēs and mēde katapraynēs render the other two verbs. Nothing is added. The Hebrew sense, three words for silence, fits the parallel lines, and Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew agrees with it.

p: Hebrew "the pastures of God"; the Greek "God's altar" (Vaticanus) or "God's sanctuary" (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew pulchritudinem Dei ("God's beauty")
readings.plain: God's grazing lands

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 82:13) (Vaticanus)
readings.plain: God's altar

readings.w: Septuagint, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus, as printed in Swete's notes; Gallican Psalter sanctuarium Dei
readings.plain: God's sanctuary

why: Ne'ot means pastures or homesteads, the land God gives his flock (79:13). The Greek copies read it as a holy place, perhaps thinking of naveh, "abode" (Exodus 15:13). Jerome took it from na'ah, "be lovely".

a: who carries the highways in the heart
p: The Hebrew says "highways in their heart"; the Greek has "he has set ascents in his heart".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew semitae in corde eius
readings.plain: who carries the highways in the heart

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 83:6); Gallican Psalter ascensiones in corde suo disposuit
readings.orig: ἀναβάσεις ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ διέθετο
readings.en: he has set ascents in his heart
readings.plain: who has set ascents in the heart

why: The Greek adds a verb and reads the roads as "ascents", the word used for the Songs of Ascents (120–134), the pilgrims' climb to Jerusalem. That is a good interpretation of the Hebrew, which is terse. The Plain keeps the Hebrew noun and supplies only "carries". The Hebrew "their" is singular in the Plain for smoothness after "anyone".

a: the early rain also wraps it in blessings
p: The Hebrew vowels read "blessings"; many read "pools". The Greek has "the lawgiver will give blessings".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the early rain also wraps (it in) blessings
readings.plain: the early rain also wraps it in blessings

readings.w: Same consonants, vowels changed (many modern translations)
readings.en: the early rain covers it with pools
readings.plain: the early rain also covers it with pools

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 83:7)
readings.orig: καὶ γὰρ εὐλογίας δώσει ὁ νομοθετῶν
readings.en: for the lawgiver will give blessings
readings.plain: the lawgiver will also give blessings

why: Berakhot, "blessings", and berekhot, "pools", are spelled alike without vowels; the context of springs suggests pools, and the Hebrew vowels may be a play on both. Moreh means "early rain" (Joel 2:23) and also "teacher", which the Greek took (Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew also has doctor, "teacher"). The Plain follows the Hebrew vowels.

a: until each one presents himself to God in Zion
t: "Appear before God" or "God will be seen"?
p: The Hebrew says each pilgrim "appears before God"; the Greek has "the God of gods will be seen in Zion".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew parebunt apud Deum
readings.en: he will appear to God in Zion
readings.plain: until each one presents himself to God in Zion

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 83:8); Gallican Psalter videbitur Deus deorum in Sion
readings.orig: ὀφθήσεται ὁ θεὸς τῶν θεῶν ἐν Σιών
readings.en: the God of gods will be seen in Zion
readings.plain: the God of gods will be seen in Zion

why: The Greek read the same letters 'l 'lhym as El elohim, "God of gods", not el elohim, "to God". The Hebrew phrase is the law's term for the pilgrimage, to "appear before the LORD" three times a year (Exodus 23:17), which the scribes may have voweled to avoid saying the pilgrims "see God".

a: The LORD God is sun and shield
p: The Hebrew calls God "sun and shield"; the Greek reads "the Lord God loves mercy and truth".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew sol et scutum
readings.en: for sun and shield is the LORD God
readings.plain: The LORD God is sun and shield

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 83:12); Gallican Psalter quia misericordiam et veritatem diligit Deus
readings.orig: ὅτι ἔλεον καὶ ἀλήθειαν ἀγαπᾷ Κύριος ὁ θεός
readings.en: for the Lord God loves mercy and truth
readings.plain: The LORD God loves mercy and truth

readings.w: Targum (checked myself)
readings.en: like a high wall and a strong shield
readings.plain: The LORD God is a high wall and a strong shield

why: The Greek translator, or his Hebrew copy, avoided calling God the sun, a name for a god in the nations around Israel; the Targum too turned it into a wall. The Hebrew is the harder reading and is supported by Jerome's translation from the Hebrew.

t: "Restored the fortunes" or "brought back the captives"?
p: The Hebrew phrase means "turned the turning" of Jacob; the Greek and Latin have "turned back the captivity of Jacob".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: you turned the turning of Jacob
readings.plain: you turned Jacob's fortunes back

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 84:2); Gallican Psalter avertisti captivitatem Iacob; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew reduxisti captivitatem Iacob
readings.en: you turned back the captivity of Jacob
readings.plain: you brought Jacob's captives back

why: Shuv shevut/shevit is an idiom for restoring someone's fortunes (Job 42:10, of Job, who was no captive). The ancient versions related shevit to shevi, "captivity", and so read the psalm as a return from exile. That may be what the poet meant, but the idiom is wider. The consonants also differ: the written text (ketiv) has shevit, the text read aloud (qere) shevut. Both are forms of the same idiom, and the Plain's wording fits either.

a: only, they must not go back to foolishness
t: "Not return to folly" or "those who turn their heart"?
p: The Hebrew warns "let them not turn back to folly". The Greek has "and to those who turn their heart to him".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and let them not turn back to folly
readings.plain: only, they must not go back to foolishness

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 84:9); Gallican Psalter et in eos qui convertuntur corde
readings.orig: καὶ τοὺς ἐπιστρέφοντας πρὸς αὐτὸν καρδίαν
readings.en: and to those who turn their heart to him
readings.plain: and to those who turn their hearts to him

why: The Greek probably read ve'el shave libbam, "to those who turn their heart", from similar letters. It is a smoother line, which is a reason to prefer the harder Hebrew. The Hebrew is supported by Jerome's translation from it (ut non convertantur ad stultitiam).

t: "Unite my heart" or "let my heart rejoice"?
p: The Hebrew says "unite my heart". The Greek, Syriac and Gallican Latin read "let my heart rejoice".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew unicum fac cor meum
readings.plain: Make my heart one

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 85:11); Gallican Psalter laetetur cor meum; Syriac, as reported in BHS (not checked myself)
readings.plain: Let my heart be glad

why: The Greek read yichad (from chadah, "rejoice") for yached, "make one". The Hebrew, a prayer for an undivided heart, matches the next words "to fear your name" and Jeremiah 32:39 ("one heart").

a: And about Zion they will say
p: The Hebrew reads "and of Zion it will be said". The Greek has "Mother Zion, a man will say".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew ad Sion autem dicetur
readings.en: and of Zion it will be said
readings.plain: And about Zion they will say

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 86:5); the Gallican Psalter has numquid Sion dicet homo, "will a man say to Zion?", reading the Greek mē for mētēr
readings.plain: "Mother Zion," each will say

why: The Greek translator read em, "mother", in the place of the Hebrew preposition, perhaps from a copy with 'm. "Mother Zion" became a favorite title in Christian hymns and fits the psalm's picture of peoples born in her (see Galatians 4:26). The Hebrew reading is shorter and stands in Jerome's translation from the Hebrew.

a: "Every spring of mine is in you."
p: The Hebrew says "all my springs are in you". The Greek has "the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew omnes fontes mei in te
readings.plain: "Every spring of mine is in you."

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 86:7); Gallican Psalter sicut laetantium omnium habitatio in te
readings.orig: ὡς εὐφραινομένων πάντων ἡ κατοικία ἐν σοί
readings.en: as of all who rejoice, the dwelling is in you
readings.plain: "All who rejoice have their home in you."

why: The Greek read me'on, "dwelling", for ma'yan, "spring", and took "singers" as "rejoicing". The Hebrew line is very short and hard, but its picture of Zion as the source of life fits 46:4 and Ezekiel 47.

a: Will the shades get up and give you thanks?
p: Hebrew refa'im, "shades". The Greek and Gallican read "physicians"; Jerome from the Hebrew, "giants".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: will shades rise, will they praise you?
readings.plain: Will the shades get up and give you thanks?

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 87:11); Gallican Psalter aut medici suscitabunt
readings.orig: ἢ ἰατροὶ ἀναστήσουσιν καὶ ἐξομολογήσονταί σοι
readings.en: or will physicians raise them up, and they will praise you?
readings.plain: Will physicians raise them up, and will they give you thanks?

readings.w: Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew aut gigantes surgent
readings.plain: Will giants get up and give you thanks?

why: The Greek read rof'im, "healers", from the same consonants. The Hebrew word for the dead is certain from Isaiah 26:14 and 26:19, which also ask whether the shades will rise. Jerome knew Refa'im as an old race of giants (Deuteronomy 2:11).

a: do you push my soul away
p: The Hebrew has "you reject my soul"; the Greek has "you reject my prayer".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew animam meam
readings.plain: do you push my soul away

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 87:15); Gallican Psalter orationem meam
readings.plain: do you push my prayer away

why: The Greek may have been influenced by "my prayer" in the verse before. The Hebrew is supported by Jerome and the Targum.

p: The Hebrew has "I have said"; the Greek and Gallican Latin have "you said", making verse 2 God's words.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: For I have said

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:3); Gallican Psalter dixisti; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew quia dixisti, as printed in Lefèvre d'Étaples' Quincuplex Psalterium (1513), checked myself (the Weber–Gryson critical text not seen)
readings.plain: For you have said

why: With "you said", God's own speech would begin at verse 2 instead of verse 3. The Hebrew has the singer state his faith in verse 2 and then quote God in verses 3–4, which is how the Plain punctuates it. The early printed text of Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew also has "you said", but it could not be checked against the modern critical edition, so it is not used here to decide the reading. The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex, as most modern translations do.

p: The Hebrew has the singular "my chosen one"; the Greek has the plural "my chosen ones".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: with the one I chose

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:4); Gallican Psalter electis meis
readings.plain: with the ones I chose

why: The Hebrew singular matches "David my servant" in the parallel line. The Greek plural may think of the people, or of the patriarchs (the Targum says Abraham).

p: The Hebrew has yamin, "right hand", that is, south. The Greek read yammim, "seas".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew aquilonem et dextram
readings.plain: North and south

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:13); Gallican Psalter aquilonem et mare
readings.plain: North and the seas

why: The two words differ by one letter, final nun or final mem, and its vowels. The Hebrew gives a natural pair of directions. Some scholars read both words as mountain names (Zaphon and Amanus), which would fit Tabor and Hermon in the next line; see the note.

a: through your favor our horn is lifted high
t: Ketiv and qere: "you lift" or "is lifted"?
p: The written Hebrew reads "you lift high our horn"; the margin, "our horn is lifted high". The Plain follows the margin.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, the reading in the margin (qere); Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:18) hypsōthēsetai; Gallican Psalter exaltabitur
readings.plain: through your favor our horn is lifted high

readings.w: Masoretic Text, the written text (ketiv); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew elevabis (in the Quincuplex Psalterium, checked myself)
readings.plain: through your favor you lift our horn high

why: Both make sense, and the difference is only a vowel letter (y or w). The margin reading matches verse 24 ("his horn will rise") and the Greek, so the Plain follows it. See the topic on ketiv and qere.

t: "Your loyal ones", "your loyal one" or "your sons"?
p: Leningrad has "your loyal ones"; many manuscripts the singular; the Greek (Vaticanus) "your sons".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew sanctis tuis
readings.plain: to your loyal ones

readings.w: Many Hebrew manuscripts, as reported in BHS (not checked myself)
readings.plain: to your loyal one

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:20) (Vaticanus); the Gallican Psalter has sanctis tuis, "your holy ones"
readings.plain: to your sons

why: The singular would point to Nathan, or to David, as the one who received the vision (2 Samuel 7:17). The plural may mean the prophets, as Rashi says (Nathan and Gad), or the faithful community that keeps the promise. The Greek "sons" is probably an interpretation. The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex.

p: Vaticanus first wrote "with holy mercy"; its corrector, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have "holy oil", as the Hebrew.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus and the corrector of Vaticanus, as printed in Swete's notes; Gallican Psalter oleo sancto meo
readings.en: with the oil of my holiness
readings.plain: with my holy oil

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:21) (first hand)
readings.plain: with holy mercy

why: Eleei, "mercy", and elaiōi, "oil", sounded almost alike in later Greek, so the Vaticanus reading is a scribal slip by ear. It is a pleasing one in a psalm about God's mercy (eleos renders hesed throughout).

p: The Hebrew has nezer, "crown". The Greek has "his holiness", the Gallican Latin "his sanctuary".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew diadema eius
readings.plain: his crown

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:40); Gallican Psalter sanctuarium eius
readings.plain: his holy thing

why: Same Hebrew, different sense: nezer means both a crown and consecration (as in "Nazirite"). The Greek took the second meaning. The Plain's "crown" fits the throne in 89:44.

p: The Hebrew is hard: "you made (him) stop from his brightness". Many emend to "his scepter".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: you have made cease from his purity
readings.plain: You have stopped his brightness

readings.w: Conjecture (dividing the letters as מַטֵּה הוֹדוֹ, "his glorious scepter")
readings.en: you have ended his glorious scepter
readings.plain: You have broken his glorious scepter

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:45); Gallican Psalter destruxisti eum ab emundatione
readings.plain: You have ended his cleansing

why: The Greek and the Targum confirm the Hebrew letters but take them as "purity"; the Targum thinks of priests who purify. The conjecture fits the throne in the next half-line but has no manuscript support. The Plain follows the Hebrew and takes tohar as "brightness", as in Exodus 24:10, and says in the note that the line is uncertain.

a: You have made his youth short
p: Hebrew "the days of his youth"; Vaticanus "the days of his throne"; other Greek copies "the days of his time".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew dies adulescentiae eius
readings.en: you have cut short the days of his youth
readings.plain: You have made his youth short

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:46)
readings.orig: ἐσμίκρυνας τὰς ἡμέρας τοῦ θρόνου αὐτοῦ
readings.en: you shortened the days of his throne
readings.plain: You have cut short the days of his throne

readings.w: Septuagint, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus, as printed in Swete's notes; Gallican Psalter dies temporis eius
readings.orig: ἐσμίκρυνας τὰς ἡμέρας τοῦ χρόνου αὐτοῦ
readings.en: you shortened the days of his time
readings.plain: You have cut short the days of his time

why: Thronou, "throne", and chronou, "time", differ by one Greek letter; one is a slip for the other, and neither renders 'alumav, "his youth", exactly. The Plain follows the Hebrew; the Plain keeps "the days of" implied in "his youth".

p: Leningrad has "your servants"; many Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac have "your servant".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:51); Gallican Psalter servorum tuorum
readings.plain: the disgrace your servants bear

readings.w: Many Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac, as reported in BHS (not checked myself)
readings.plain: the disgrace your servant bears

why: The singular would match "David your servant" (89:3, 20, 39) and the "I" in the next half-line. The plural makes the king's shame the people's shame. Both fit; the Plain follows the Leningrad Codex and the Greek.

a: at the footprints of your anointed
p: Hebrew "the heels (footprints) of your anointed"; Greek "the exchange (antallagma) of your christ".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew vestigia christi tui
readings.plain: at the footprints of your anointed

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 88:52); Gallican Psalter commutationem christi tui
readings.plain: at the price paid for your anointed

why: 'Eqev also means "reward, wages, consequence" (19:11), and the Greek took that sense: "exchange" or "price". The Hebrew picture of enemies mocking the king's every step is simpler. The Targum ("the delay of the footsteps of your Messiah") and the rabbis built on the Hebrew; see the notes.

p: The Hebrew has haggittit; the Greek and Latin read gittot, "for the winepresses". So also at 84:0.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: On the gittith

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek; Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus, checked myself) (Psalm 80:1) and 83:1 (Hebrew 84:0); Gallican Psalter pro torcularibus; Jerome's Psalter from the Hebrew in torcularibus
readings.plain: On the winepresses

why: The Hebrew letters gtyt could be voweled as a plural of gat, "winepress". The Greek reading is an interpretation of the same letters. The Plain keeps the unexplained Hebrew word; see the note.

a: Yet my loyal love I will not break off from him
p: The Leningrad Codex has afir, "I will break off"; some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac have asir, "I will remove".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and my loyal love I will not break off from him
readings.plain: Yet my loyal love I will not break off from him

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac, as reported in BHS (not checked myself)
readings.en: and my loyal love I will not remove from him
readings.plain: Yet my loyal love I will not take away from him

why: Asir, "remove", is the verb of 2 Samuel 7:15 (lo yasur) and 1 Chronicles 17:13 (lo asir), so it may be a scribe's harmonizing with those texts. Afir, "break, annul", is the harder reading and matches the covenant language of the psalm ("My covenant I will not profane", 89:34). The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex.
